subject: english-language
topicDisplay: Paper 1 Non Fiction Texts And Transactional Writing
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: An advert claims its drink is "loved by champions everywhere." The phrase "loved by champions" is an example of:
questions.explain: A vague, flattering and unsourced claim is persuasion rather than verifiable fact.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of a discourse marker such as 'however' or 'furthermore'?
options: To signal the relationship between ideas and guide the reader
questions.explain: Discourse markers connect ideas and show contrast, addition or sequence to aid coherence.

questions.q: You are writing a magazine article. Which feature is most typical of the article form?
options: An engaging headline and a subheading that draws the reader in
A scene number and act heading
A signed-off complimentary close like 'Yours sincerely'
questions.explain: Articles use headlines and subheadings to grab attention and signpost content.

questions.q: "Picture yourself sinking into warm golden sand as gentle waves lap at your feet." The main method used to persuade here is:
options: Appealing imagery that helps the reader imagine the scene
questions.explain: Vivid sensory imagery invites the reader to picture and desire the experience.

questions.q: You are writing a leaflet for a local charity event. Which feature is most appropriate to the form?
options: A single dense block of text
Clear headings, bullet points and key details like time and place
questions.explain: Leaflets use headings, bullets and signposting so readers can scan key information quickly.

questions.q: Two articles discuss zoos: one calls them "vital sanctuaries," the other "cruel prisons." Comparing these word choices shows the writers differ mainly in their:
options: Viewpoint and the connotations of the words they choose
questions.explain: Contrasting loaded word choices ("sanctuaries" vs "prisons") reveal opposing viewpoints and connotations.

questions.q: When writing to advise, which tone is usually most effective?
options: Reassuring and constructive, offering clear guidance
questions.explain: Writing to advise works best with a supportive, constructive tone that guides the reader.

questions.q: To SYNTHESISE information from two sources, you should:
options: List every word in both texts
Combine relevant points from both into a single, linked explanation
questions.explain: Synthesis means drawing together and connecting information from both texts.

questions.q: Addressing the reader as "you" in a persuasive article is known as:
questions.explain: Speaking straight to the reader using "you" is direct address.

questions.q: In persuasive writing, what is the effect of using a rule of three (a triplet)?
options: It removes the need for evidence
It signals the end of the piece
It makes the writing harder to read
It creates rhythm and emphasis, making the point more memorable
questions.explain: A triplet adds rhythm and emphasis, making ideas stick in the reader's mind.

questions.q: "Year after year, ton after ton, our oceans drown in plastic." The repetition of "after" mainly works to:
options: Stress the relentless, ongoing scale of the problem
questions.explain: Repeating "after" emphasises a continuous, mounting build-up, stressing the scale.

questions.q: Which is the best way to adapt your writing for a young child as the audience?
options: Use long, complex sentences and abstract vocabulary
Write in a formal, legalistic register
Use simple, clear sentences, friendly tone and concrete vocabulary
Include dense statistics and technical jargon
questions.explain: Writing for young children needs simple sentences, a warm tone and accessible words.

questions.q: A writer's TONE in "I suppose, if one absolutely must, one could call this 'art'" is best described as:
questions.explain: The reluctant phrasing and scare-quotes around "art" convey sarcasm and dismissal.

questions.q: You are writing a speech. Which feature would make it most engaging for a live audience?
options: Long, unbroken paragraphs of dense detail
A repeated phrase used as a rallying refrain
questions.explain: Repetition (anaphora) builds rhythm and impact, ideal for spoken delivery.

questions.q: Which sentence is the strongest example of using a metaphor in descriptive writing?
options: The night sky was dark, with some stars showing.
The night sky was a black ocean drowning every star.
The night sky was very dark and a bit cloudy.
The night sky looked like it had stars in it.
questions.explain: Calling the sky 'a black ocean' directly identifies it as something else, creating a vivid metaphor.

questions.q: Identifying a writer's VIEWPOINT means working out:
options: Their attitude or opinion towards the subject
questions.explain: Viewpoint is the writer's stance or attitude on the topic.

questions.q: A leaflet tells readers "Always wear a helmet and check your brakes." Its main purpose is to:
questions.explain: Practical guidance and instructions for the reader's benefit show the purpose is to advise.

questions.q: You are writing a review of a film. Which feature suits the form best?
options: A formal salutation and address block
A balanced judgement supported by specific examples and a recommendation
questions.explain: Reviews give an evaluative judgement backed by examples and end with a recommendation.

questions.q: Which is the clearest sign of the intended AUDIENCE in "Top tips for surviving your first term at uni"?
options: Casual language and the reference to "uni" suggest young/new students
It is aimed at retired people
questions.explain: Informal tone and student-focused content signal a young, new-undergraduate audience.

questions.q: "It was cruel, heartless and utterly inhumane." The use of three linked words for emphasis is called:
questions.explain: Three items grouped for rhetorical force is tripling (a triplet/rule of three).

questions.q: "Over 90% of teachers agree that homework helps." Which persuasive device is used here?
questions.explain: A figure or percentage used to support a point is a statistic.

questions.q: Which technique is being used: 'Imagine a world where no child goes to bed hungry'?
options: Direct address and an emotive appeal
questions.explain: It speaks directly to the reader ('Imagine') and triggers an emotional response.

specSource: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE English Language (Spec A) (4EA1) specification; Paper 1 Non Fiction Texts And Transactional Writing
